query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A physics‐informed machine learning model that incorporates key descriptors from the hierarchical heterostructure (such as local elastic constants, interfacial energies, and misfit volumes from nanoscale features) can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture tests more rapidly and with improved accuracy compared to conventional DFT/MD simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy in its as‐fabricated state exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure that includes nanoscale precipitates, grain boundaries, and interfacial regions.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a multiscale predictive framework combining machine learning feature selection (using physics‐based descriptors from the hierarchical microstructure) with streamlined atomistic calculations.
generation.conditions: Quasi‐static tensile and fracture testing at room temperature; calibration is based on low to moderate strain rates where the heterostructure governs the deformation response.
generation.structural_mediator: The hierarchical interfaces and nanometer‐scale precipitates mediate local stress redistributions, control dislocation mobility, and act as barriers to fracture propagation.
generation.mechanism: By quantifying descriptors such as local elastic moduli, interfacial energies, and misfit volumes from the heterostructure, the model can efficiently capture stress transfer and dislocation interactions that dominate the elastic and fracture response. This targeted feature integration reduces computational expense while preserving critical physical insights lost in broader simulation approaches.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model is expected to reduce computational simulation time by roughly 50–70% and achieve predictive error margins for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture parameters that are 10–20% lower than those obtained from conventional DFT/MD simulations.
generation.baseline: Established full-scale atomistic simulations (DFT/MD) that are computationally intensive and may inadequately resolve heterostructural effects, resulting in higher predictive variability.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may fail under conditions where the heterostructure dynamics are dominated by extreme strain rates, elevated temperatures, or unanticipated long‐range interactions that are not captured by the selected descriptors or training dataset.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage gains in accuracy and efficiency are uncertain due to the limited calibration data specific to HfNbTiVAl10, and the model’s performance under dynamic or off‐design loading conditions may deviate from predictions.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct independent quasi‐static tensile and fracture tests on HfNbTiVAl10 samples while simultaneously using the physics‐informed machine learning model to predict mechanical properties based on microstructural descriptors measured from the same alloy. Compare the measured properties with model predictions.
measurements: Young’s modulus via stress–strain curve slope in the elastic regime
Yield strength determined by a 0.2% offset method
Fracture parameters (e.g., fracture toughness, elongation at break) from standardized fracture tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the ML model’s predictions deviate by more than 30% from the independently measured values or if the computational time savings compared to conventional DFT/MD simulations are less than 20%.

cited_evidence.text: A typical method of choice for truly predictive calculations of alloy properties is density functional theory (DFT). However, explicit evaluation of fracture or yield strength in alloys is mostly out of reach for available DFT implementations. Although this may become possible with general-purpose interatomic potentials,, a fairly robust description can be obtained by using appropriate models, which have been shown to accurately predict strengthening and ductility. These models combine linear elasticity and microscopic principles, and the only required input parameters are certain material properties. Specifically, apart from basic equilibrium properties, such as the molar volume and elastic constants, the strengthening model requires misfit volumes related to concentration derivatives of the alloy volume, while the ductility model relies on surface and unstable stacking fault (USF) energies computed for specific orientations. Importantly, all of these parameters are accessible through simulations using first-principles methods, yet, such simulations are still challenging for disordered MPEAs.

Machine learning (ML) has emerged as an indispensable tool in computational materials science, offering the ability to analyze extensive datasets, identify complex patterns, and predict properties based on input features. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of ML in predicting HEA properties [,,,,,,,,,]. These studies typically involve the collection of extensive experimental data, the selection of relevant features, and the development of predictive models using various ML algorithms. For instance, Sengupta et al. [] employed a Neural Network model to predict the yield strength and plasticity of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), using elemental composition and physics-based properties as features. This study also highlighted the role of uncertainty quantification in enhancing predictive reliability.

AbstractA hierarchical microstructure strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with superior cost specific yield strength from room temperature up to 1,023 K is presented. By phase transformation pathway through metastability, HESA possesses a hierarchical microstructure containing a dispersion of nano size disordered FCC particles inside ordered L12 precipitates that are within the FCC matrix. The average tensile yield strength of HESA from room temperature to 1,023 K could be 120 MPa higher than that of advanced single crystal superalloy, while HESA could still exhibit an elongation greater than 20%. Furthermore, the cost specific yield strength of HESA can be 8 times that of some superalloys. A template for lighter, stronger, cheaper, and more ductile high temperature alloy is proposed.Subject terms: Mechanical properties, Metals and alloys
